title: A signal in the wrong direction
brief:
This chart shows the monthly **catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) rate** per 1,000 catheter-days (lower is better). The median is the dashed line.

A colleague says: 'Six months in a row above the line — at least it's consistent.' Read the chart and decide what it really means.

task.stem: What does this pattern tell you?

options.label: Good news — the rate is stable and consistent; no action needed.
A real signal in the undesirable direction — a sustained upward shift. Investigate what changed around M9 and act.
Just noise — every month varies; ignore it.
An improvement — six months in a row is a good run.

reasons.label: A run of six or more points on one side of the median is a shift — and direction matters. Here the shift is upward on a 'lower-is-better' measure, so it demands investigation and action, not reassurance.
Any movement on a chart means the process is out of control and must be stopped.
An upward run is always a good sign.
You must always wait for at least 24 points before reading any signal.

debrief.correct: Exactly. From M9, eight consecutive months sit **above** the median (3.0) — a clear **shift**. A shift is a real special-cause signal, but **direction matters**: on a lower-is-better measure like CAUTI, an upward shift is a deterioration, not a 'consistent' or 'good' run. The right move is to investigate what changed around M9 (a new catheter practice? a staffing change? a supply switch?) and act. Reading the direction wrong is how teams celebrate a signal that should alarm them.
debrief.wrong: Two things to get right. First, this **is** a signal: eight months in a row above the median is a shift (six or more on one side). Second, and just as important, the **direction**: CAUTI is a lower-is-better measure, so an upward shift is a worsening. It is neither noise to ignore nor good news to celebrate — investigate what changed around M9 and act.
debrief.rule_cited: Shift rule and the importance of direction — Provost & Murray (2nd ed.), IHI QI 104.
